newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire thrust meets resistance, rebels say blocked.
newsitem.headline: Zaire thrust meets resistance, rebels say blocked.

text.p: Zaire's mercenary-backed army has run into stiff resistance in its bid to recapture towns and territory from rebels in the east, sources say.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, speaking on French radio, said on Friday that his forces had blocked Zaire's much-trumpeted counter-offensive.
"We have stopped the famous counter-offensive which we have totally wiped out," Kabila said in an interview broadcast on Radio France Internationale from Goma, eastern Zaire.
"We control the territory... In the last two days there have been no more battles. We have discovered that the enemy has retreated considerably due to the losses," he said.
Earlier, military and other sources reported Zairean troops fighting on several fronts, with rebels heading towards the mineral-producing southern Shaba province.
"We are having to fight on several fronts," said a defence ministry official, who asked not to be identified.
Tutsi-led rebels launched the offensive in October accusing Zaire of denying them citizenship and seeking to expel them.
Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and his government launched a counter-attack on January 20. Mobutu is in France for fresh medical tests following cancer surgery last August.
Kabila told French radio his aim was not to go as far as Kisangani, the headquarters of the Zairean offensive, and he repeated calls for negotiations.
"We want these gentlemen to come and sit down at a negotiating table rather than go back to their wily old ways," he said.

Zaire's government has ruled out negotiations, saying troops from neighbouring countries must leave first. "The government will not negotiate with the aggressors until we have recovered all the territory that has been occupied," Deputy Foreign Minister Henri Thomas Lokondo Yoka said on Thursday.
Zaire accuses Rwanda, Burundi and most recently Uganda of invading to back the rebels.
All three deny their troops are fighting inside Zaire.
France and former colonial power Belgium have both expressed concern about the likelihood of foreign troops fighting alongside the rebels.
African jurists meeting in Senegal's capital Dakar added their voice to the expressions of concern.

Zaire's army spoke on Thursday of fighting near Watsa and Isiro, hundreds of km (miles) into Upper Zaire province. Military sources told Reuters earlier Zairean soldiers and foreign mercenaries were based in Watsa.
Some sources said Watsa had already fallen.
The army accused Rwandan troops of fighting on the road from Walekale, just over 100 km (70 miles) from the Rwandan border, to Kisangani.

A French foreign ministry spokesman said France had no concrete evidence of direct involvement of Zaire's neighbours in the fighting but expressed concern at the "multiplication of signs" suggesting this.

The U.N. Refugee Agency in Geneva said local Zairean authorities in the Lubutu area had told relief agencies to stop work in the area and had banned U.N. planes from landing. The reasons were not immediately clear.
